prefercite.head: Preferred Citation
prefercite.p: Charlotte County (Va.) Business Records, 1815-1939, undated. Local government records collection, Charlotte County Court Records. The Library of Virginia, Richmond, Va. 23219.

acqinfo.head: Acquisition Information
acqinfo.p: These records came to the Library of Virginia in transfers of court papers from Charlotte County in an undated accession.
Watkins and Jones Account Book and Daybook, 1877-1885, with accession number 21697, was originally transferred to the Library of Virginia with Rockbridge County Circuit Court records.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: Prior to 2024, the various business records in this collection were originally described as individual records, but they have been consolidated into one large business record for the locality.

bioghist.head: Historical Information
bioghist.p: Context for Record Type: Business Records, both volumes and loose records, are in some cases transferred to the Library of Virginia as components of court record transfers. These business records in some cases were simply stored in the local court building for safe keeping by business owners. In other cases, business records (particularly ledgers, account books, etc.) may have been filed in a court case as an exhibit. These business record exhibits appeared both in chancery causes and in judgments, these records serving as exhibits for business dissolution cases, debt suits, and contract disputes.

Locality History:Charlotte County was named for Charlotte Sophia of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, wife of King George III. It was formed from Lunenburg County in 1764. The county court first met on 5 March 1765. The county seat is Charlotte Court House. Area: 475 square miles. Population: 12,471 (2000), 12,700 (2005 estimate.)

scopecontent.head: Scope and Content
scopecontent.p: Charlotte County (Va.) Business Records, 1815-1939, undated, are comprised of various records created by individuals and companies in pursuit of documenting business activities in and around Charlotte County (Va.) Represented records consist of bound volumes such as a minute book, ledgers, daybooks, bills receivable books, blotters and ticklers, checkbooks, drafts, journals, cashbooks, account books and a memorandum book.

did.unittitle: Appomattox and Charlotte Railway Company Minute Book, 1905

scopecontent.p: Historical Information:The Appomattox and Charlotte Railway Company was incorporated on September 11, 1905, at Charlotte Courthouse. The stockholders created a Board of Directors and established its authority.
Scope and Content:Appomattox and Charlotte Railway Company Minute Book, 1905, records the first meeting of the company's stockholders.

did.unittitle: Appomattox and Charlotte Railway Company Minute Book 1905

scopecontent.p: Historical Information:A business identified by the initial C and M may have operated in Charlotte County in the mid-to late 19th century.

Scope and Content:C and M Ledger, 1861-1874, records the accounts of individual customers. Each account lists transactions in chronological order and the amount owed and paid. Ledger does not list the names of items purchased, rather it used the general term "merchandise". Ledger also records the company's controlling accounts such as profit and loss and interest accounts.
Historical Information:Cary and Bradley were tailors operating in Charlotte County during the early 19th century. Their shop may have been named Cary and Bradley.

Scope and Content:Cary and Bradley Ledger, 1842-1843, records the individual accounts of customers. Each account lists transactions in chronological order, services rendered, and amount owed or paid. Services rendered include altering pants, mending clothes, putting straps on pants, and making vests and coats.

Historical Information:Chappell and Fuqua was a mercantile partnership formed by Josiah W. Chappell and Samuel S. Fuqua and conducted business in Charlotte County during the early 19th century. Before May 1832, Chappell and Fuqua was known as Samuel S. Fuqua and Company.
Scope and Content:The Chappell and Fuqua Records, 1832-1839, are comprised of a daybook and a ledger.

Chappell and Fuqua Daybook, 1832-1833, records daily transactions as they occurred in 1832-1833. Information found in each entry includes name of customer, items sold, and amount owed or paid. Merchandise sold includes dry goods, whiskey, spices, farm tools, vegetables, and paper.

Chappell and Fuqua Ledger, 1833-1839, records the individual accounts of customers. Each account lists transactions in chronological order, items purchased, and amount owed and paid. Merchandise sold includes whiskey, molasses, shoes, cups, saucers, and straw hats. Payments were made by cash or barter such as a horse collar, hay, grass seed, and bacon.
See also: Charlotte County Chancery Cause, Martin Hancock and others vs. Samuel S. Fugua and others, 1841-004. Available Digitally through the Chancery Records Index.

did.unittitle: Charlotte Banking and Insurance Company Records, 1872-1909

scopecontent.p: Historical Information:In 1909 S. C. Daniel was appointed trustee to oversee the assets of the Charlotte Banking and Insurance Company. After the bank became insolvent, Daniel was unwilling to assume the responsibility of administering the said trust without protection from the Charlotte County Circuit Court.

Scope and Content:The Charlotte Banking and Insurance Company Records, 1872-1909, consist of two Bills Receivable Ledgers, nine Blotter and Ticklers, three Cashier's Books, two Checkbooks, two Daybooks, one book of Drafts, eleven Journals and four Ledgers.

Charlotte Banking and Insurance Company Bills Receivable Ledgers, 1883-1902, record information related to promissory notes held by individual customers. It lists the date note was issued, number of notes, name of customer, endorser of note, payment period, date payment was due, total amount of note, interest on note, and remarks on whether note was paid, renewed, consolidated, etc.

scopecontent.p: Charlotte Banking and Insurance Company Blotter and Ticklers, 1872-1889, 1891-1898, record daily within each month the company's sundry financial activities involving bills receivable, interest accounts, stocks, payments, and notes due. A blotter and tickler is like a daybook. It is a single-entry journal in which transactions and obligations are entered as they take place, usually pending their transfer to permanent record books.

Charlotte Banking and Insurance Company Blotter and Tickler Book, 1902-1903, records the company's sundry financial activities involving bills receivable, interest accounts, stocks, payments, and notes due. Entries include name of individual or company, and underneath name of individual or company, the date and style of transaction or obligation. Although titled "Blotter and Tickler", entries were entered not by date of transaction or obligation as normally found in a blotter and tickler but by name of individual or company.

scopecontent.p: Historical Information:William W. Crawley operated a general store at the Charlotte Court House in the early 19th century.

Scope and Content:William W. Cashbook, 1846-1849, records daily cash received and cash paid out by his general store. It also lists names of individuals Crawley received cash from and paid cash to. Merchandise sold includes chickens, eggs, vinegar, horse feed, dry goods, peaches, and soap.

did.unittitle: Cronin and Company Ledgers and Index, 1865-1868, undated

scopecontent.p: Historical Information:Cronin and Company was a mercantile partnership owned by Robert W. Cronin and others that conducted business in Charlotte County during the mid-19th century.

Scope and Content:Cronin and Company Ledgers A-1 and B, 1865-1868, record the accounts of individual customers. Each account lists transactions in chronological order, items purchased, and the amount owed and paid. Merchandise sold includes whiskey, dry goods, eggs, nails, fishhooks, and farm tools. The Index, which refers to the ledgers, is undated.
See also: Charlotte County Chancery Cause, Administrator of James Maloney versus Cronin, Hannah, and Company, 1871-001. Available Digitally through the Chancery Records Index.

did.unittitle: Cronin and Company Index to Ledger undated

scopecontent.p: Historical Information:: Cronin, Hannah, and Company was a general store that conducted business in the town of Coles Finz during the mid to late 19th century. The partnership was comprised of Robert W. Cronin, George C. Hannah, and Benjamin W. Marshall.

Scope and Content:: Cronin, Hannah and Company Journal, 1861-1864, 1874 records monthly, mainly in 1861, the individual accounts of customers. Each account lists transactions in chronological order, items purchased, and amount owed or paid. Merchandise sold includes dry goods (thread, calico, needles, buttons), molasses, pants, castor oil, and whiskey.

Cronin, Hannah, and Company Cashbook, 1861-1870, records on an almost daily basis cash received and cash paid out. It includes the names of individuals the business received cash from and paid cash to.
See also: Charlotte County Chancery Cause, Administrator of James Maloney versus Cronin, Hannah, and Company, 1871-001. Available Digitally through the Chancery Records Index.
The cashbook of Cronin, Hannah, and Company was used as evidence in the above cited chancery case heard in Charlotte County Circuit Court.

did.unittitle: M. B. and E General Store Records, 1856-1858

scopecontent.p: Historical Information:: A general store whose initials were M. B. and E. operated in Charlotte County during the mid-19th century.

Scope and Content:M. B. and E. General Store Ledger A, 1856-1858, records the accounts of individual customers. Beside each entry is a page number found in corresponding Journal B where the customer's specific transactions can be found. Each account lists transactions in chronological order and the amount owed and paid. Ledger also records the company's controlling accounts such as expense account, merchandise account, interest account, and profit and loss account.

M. B. and E. General Store Journal B, 1857-1858, records accounts of individual customers monthly. Beside each entry is the page number where the customer's complete account is found in corresponding Ledger A. Information found in each entry is the date of transaction, items purchased, and the amount owed and paid. Merchandise sold include socks, shoes, nails, turpentine, sugar, champagne, and whiskey.

scopecontent.p: Historical Information:David Holmes Morton was a prominent merchant in Charlotte County, Virginia. He either owned or was a partner in several mercantile businesses.

Scope and Content:David Holmes Morton Daybook, 1859-1863, records transactions daily as they occurred in the months of September 1859-Febraury 1860, May 1860, and July-December 1863. Information found in each entry includes name of customer, items purchased, and the amount owed or paid. Merchandise sold include whiskey, clothing, nails, dry-goods, and kerosene. Volume includes an inventory of store merchandise taken in July 1863. Also includes a listing of merchandise sold at auctions held by David Holmes Morton in January and May 1863 and Smith and Company in April and June 1863. Merchandise sold at the auctions were mostly household items such as mouse traps, waffle irons, and plates.

David Holmes Morton Daybook, 1861-1864, records transactions daily as they occurred in the months of January, March, May, July, September, and November. Information found in each entry includes name of customer and the amount owed and paid. Merchandise sold includes cloth, dishes, linen, shoes, pins, buttons, and whiskey.

David Holmes Morton Journal B, 1861-1865, records monthly the accounts of individual customers. Each account lists in chronological order the customers transactions for that month, items purchased, and the amount owed and paid. Also, the March, May, July, and September entries include page numbers that correspond with entries found in daybook.
See also: Charlotte County Chancery Cause, David and Wood versus D. H. Morton and others, 1890-010. Available Digitally through the Chancery Records Index.

Historical Information:Morton, Bouldin, and Gaines was a general store that conducted business during the mid-nineteenth century in Charlotte County. William Old Bouldin and David H. Morton were two of the partners. Bouldin also served a term as sheriff of Charlotte County.
David Holmes Morton was a prominent merchant in Charlotte County, Virginia. He either owned or was a partner in several mercantile businesses.
Scope and Content:Morton, Bouldin, and Gaines Ledger, 1853-1859, is a cash book that records cash on hand and cash received on the debit side and cash paid out on the credit side.
See also: Charlotte County Chancery Cause, David and Wood versus D. H. Morton and others, 1890-010. Available Digitally through the Chancery Records Index.

did.unittitle: Planters National Bank of Keysville Day Journal, 1934-1939

scopecontent.p: Historical Information:The Planters National Bank of Keysville operated in Charlotte County in the early 20th century.

Scope and Content:Charlotte County (Va.) Planters National Bank of Keysville Day Journal, 1934-1939, records daily entry of individual customers who are making deposits or receiving loans and the bank's controlling accounts such as expense account, cash account, rent, and interest account. There is also a listing of cash received and disbursements. Information found in each entry includes date, type, and amount of financial transactions and names of individuals involved. Volume contains numerous loose papers (receivers' reports, copies of decree, and deposit slips) related to the chancery case.
The Day Journal was perhaps used as evidence in a chancery case, State Corporation Commission of Virginia vs. Planters National Bank of Keysville, Inc.

scopecontent.p: Historical Information:: An unidentified General Store with initials R. W. C. operated in Charlotte County during the mid to late 19th century.

Scope and Content:: R. W. C. Ledger A, 1869-1871, records the accounts of individual customers. Each account lists transactions in chronological order and the amount owed and paid. Merchandise sold includes cloth, nails, eggs, soap, sugar, chickens, and clothing.
Historical Information:Historical Information: Captain William Smith owned a tavern located in the town of Charlotte Court House during the early to mid-nineteenth century.
Scope and Content:Captain William Smith Tavern Records, 1831-1851, consist of 13 ledgers and 2 daybooks.

Captain William Smith Tavern Ledgers, 1831-1851, list the accounts of individual customers. The ledgers record in chronological order the amount owed, and the amount paid for drinks, meals, care of horses, lodging and other expenses. Payments were made by cash, by barter such as oats and hay, and by labor such as hauling ice and barrels of whiskey. Drinks served include beer, whiskey, brandy, wine, and cider.

Captain William Smith Tavern Daybooks, 1835, 1850-1851, record daily transactions. Information includes names of customers, and the amount owed and paid. Transactions include payments for drinks, meals, care of horses, lodging and other expenses. Payments were made by cash and by labor such as hauling barrels of whiskey. Drinks served include beer, whiskey, brandy, wine, and cider.

Historical Information:Smith, Booker, and Company was a general store that conducted business during the early 19th century in the town of Charlotte Courthouse. Two of the partners in the store were John Booker and William A. Smith.

Scope and Content:Smith, Booker, and Company Daybook, 1847, records transactions daily as they occurred in March-September 1847. Information found in each entry includes name of customer, items purchased, and the amount owed or paid. Merchandise sold includes candles, pocketknives, molasses, tea, cologne, sugar, and dry goods. Volume includes a few loose documents--wills and estate records.

Historical Information:Spencer and Company was a general store that conducted business in the mid-19th century in the town of Charlotte Court House. Thomas J. Spencer was the primary owner of the store.
Scope and Content:Smith and Company Records, 1852-1867, consist of a ledger and 4 daybooks and a journal.

Spencer and Company Ledger, 1852-1858, records the accounts of individual customers. Each account lists transactions in chronological order and the amount owed and paid. The ledger does not list the names of items purchased, rather it uses the general term "merchandise." The ledger also records the company's controlling accounts such as profit and loss and interest accounts.

Spencer and Company Daybook, 1859, records transactions daily as they occurred from January-November 1859. Information found in each entry includes name of customer, items purchased, and amount owed or paid. Merchandise sold includes bacon, lamps, candles, shoes, nails, hats, and rice.

Spencer and Company Daybook, 1860, records transactions daily as they occurred from January-November 1860. Information found in each entry includes name of customer, items purchased, and amount owed or paid. Merchandise sold includes bacon, cologne, scissors, shoes, nails, hoop skirts, and molasses.

Spencer and Company Daybook, 1860, records monthly the individual accounts of customers. Each account lists in chronological order merchandise purchased by the customer that month and the amount owed and paid. Beside each transaction entry is the page number where the transaction can be found in the first volume.

Spencer and Company Daybook, 1861-1862, records transactions daily as they occurred from February 1861-April 1862. Information found in each entry includes name of customer, items purchased, and amount owed or paid. Merchandise sold includes pepper, suspenders, pane glass, dry goods, nails, shot, and molasses.

Spencer and Company Journal records monthly the individual accounts of customers from 1861-1867. Each account lists in chronological order merchandise purchased by the customer that month and the amount owed and paid. Beside each transaction entry found in accounts from February 1861-April 1862 is the page number where the transaction can be found in the daybook.
Historical Information:Spencer, Garden, and Company was a general store that conducted business at Charlotte Court House. Thomas J. Spencer was one of the partners in the store.

Scope and Content:Spencer, Garden, and Company Journals, 1855, 1857-1858, record monthly the individual accounts of customers from May-December 1855 and March 1857-December 1858. Each account lists in chronological order merchandise purchased by the customer that month and the amount owed or paid. Merchandise sold includes velvet slippers, toothbrushes, dry goods, candles, cheese, tools, coffee, and sugar.
Historical Information:John Thomas operated an unidentified business in Charlotte County in the early 19th century.

Scope and Content:John Thomas Ledger, 1815-1818, records the individual accounts of customers. Each account lists transactions in chronological order and the page numbers of other ledgers where a detailed entry of the transactions can be found.
Historical Information:John Henry Thomas was a buyer for the Richmond and Danville Railroad in Charlotte County in the mid-19th century.

Scope and Content:John Henry Thomas Account Book, 1853-1854, records purchases of goods by Thomas on behalf of the ninetieth section of the Richmond & Danville Railroad to give to rail workers and horses. It includes the accounts of individuals and businesses that Thomas purchased goods from. Each account lists transactions in chronological order, goods purchased, and amount owed or paid. Goods purchased include corn, flour, wheat, oats, rice, sugar, bacon, and coffee.
Historical Information:An unidentified Blacksmith shop operated in Charlotte County in the early 19th century.

Scope and Content:Unidentified Blacksmith Daybook, 1828, records transactions daily as they occurred. Information found in each entry includes name of customer, service provided, and the amount owed or paid. Services performed by the blacksmith shop included making ox rings, pointing farm instruments, shoeing horses, and making chains.
Historical Information:: An unidentified bank or investment business operated in Charlotte County in the early 20th century.

Scope and Content:Unidentified Business Ledger, 1919-1925, records the accounts of individual customers. Each account lists transactions in chronological order and the amount owed and paid. The volume also records the business' controlling accounts such as expenses, unpaid accounts and deposits.
Historical Information:An unidentified doctor practiced in Charlotte County in the early 19th century.

Scope and Content:Unidentified Doctor Ledger, 1819-1822, records the accounts of individual customers. The accounts list charges and payments for visits to patients, medication, and other medical services such as extracting teeth and visits to ill enslaved individuals.
Historical Information:An unidentified general store operated int the town of Rough Creek in Charlotte County in the mid-19th century.

Scope and Content:Unidentified General Store Daybook, 1866, records transactions daily as they occurred in June-November 1866. Information found in each entry includes name of customer, items purchased, and the amount owed or paid. Merchandise sold includes shot, whiskey, matches, shoes, bacon, candles, and coffee.
Historical Information:An unidentified general store operated in the town of Red Oak Grove in Charlotte County in the early 19th century.

Scope and Content:Unidentified General Store Journal A, 1831-1832, records the individual accounts of customers. Each account lists transactions in chronological order, items purchased, and the amount owed or paid. Merchandise sold includes brandy, dry goods, nails, molasses, clothing, and gun powder.
Historical Information:An unidentified general store operated in Charlotte County in the mid-19th century.
Scope and Content:Unidentified General Store Ledger A, 1856-1869, records the accounts of individual customers. Each account lists transactions in chronological order and the amount owed and paid.
Historical Information:An unidentified agency that oversaw the financial status of businesses and merchants operated in Charlotte County in the late 19th century.

Scope and Content:Unidentified Memorandum Book, 1874-1882, records the financial status of businesses and merchants in Charlotte County. Entries underneath name of business or merchant are entered in chronological order and contain critical remarks regarding their credit, financial worth, and work ethic.
Historical Information:J. J. Ward operated and owned a blacksmith shop in Charlotte County in the mid-19th century.

Scope and Content:J. J. Ward Daybook, 1855, records transactions daily as they occurred. Information found in each entry includes name of customer, services rendered, and the amount owed or paid. Services rendered include shoeing horses, sharpening farm tools, repairing wagon wheels, and making screws and nails.

did.unittitle: Watkins and Jones Account Book and Daybook, 1877-1885

scopecontent.p: Historical Information:Watkins and Jones was a law partnership located at Charlotte Court House, Virginia in the late 19th century that consisted of Isaac R. Watkins and Thomas N. Jones. Watkins and Jones heard cases in various localities in Virginia including Charlotte County, Halifax County, Cumberland County, Dinwiddie County, and Prince Edward County.

Scope and Content:Watkins and Jones Account Book and Daybook, 1877-1885, records the transactions of the law partnership. The account book portion of the volume records the expense accounts of the law partners. Each account lists transactions in chronological order. Information found in each entry includes date of transaction, expenses rendered, amount owed, form of payment, and amount paid. Types of expenses include office rent, payment for servants, and postage. The daybook portion of the volume records in chronological order court cases involving Watkins and Jones. Information found in entries include term of court when suit was heard, style of suit, and summary of suit. Types of suits include criminal, judgments and chancery. The volume also lists the sale of Thomas N. Jones' personal property on November 28, 1885. It records the name of the purchaser, items purchased, and amount paid.
See also: Charlotte County Chancery Cause, Tucker C. Watkins and wife, etc. versus Administrator of Thomas N. Jones, etc, 1894-009. Available Digitally through the Chancery Records Index.
The Watkins and Jones Account Book was used as an exhibit in the above cited case.
